title: the Gayatri in context
hook: open the Rig Veda to the Gayatri and look for om bhur bhuvah svah. it isn't in the verse

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri in context: a verse named for its meter, three short lines, and called the Savitri in older law books. Did you catch something named for its shape? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-five.

Open the Rig Veda to book three, hymn sixty-two, verse ten. Run a finger along the line, looking for the words that often come first when the Gayatri is chanted: Om bhur bhuvah svah. They aren't there. The verse in the Rig Veda begins tat savitur varenyam. The opening so often chanted with it sits outside the verse, like a doorway built in front of a house. Today: the words before the Gayatri, and why they're said.
screen: `BOOK THREE, HYMN SIXTY-TWO, VERSE TEN.` → `OM BHUR BHUVAH SVAH: NOT THERE.` → `A DOORWAY IN FRONT OF THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: When the Gayatri is recited in daily practice, it's often framed. First comes Om, the sacred syllable. Then three short words: bhur, bhuvah, svah. These are called vyahritis, utterances. They aren't part of the Rig Veda verse; they come from the practice of reciting it, and from other Vedic texts that talk about them. One of those is the Taittiriya Upanishad. In paraphrase, it says: bhur, bhuvah, suvar, these are the three utterances. Then it says a teacher named Mahachamasya made known a fourth, mahas. And it lays them out like a map. Bhur is this world, the earth. Bhuvah is the space in between. Suvar is the world beyond. And mahas, it says, is the sun. So before a person asks the sun to stir their thoughts, they first name where they stand. The ground. The air. The sky. In three words they've walked from the earth under their feet up to the heavens, and only then do they turn to Savitr. That's the frame. Om, then the three worlds, then the verse. Some recitations add more, but that is the core of the frame. It matters for context. When someone says, the Gayatri goes Om bhur bhuvah svah, tat savitur varenyam, they're not wrong about how it's chanted. They're describing the practice, a living tradition of its own. The Rig Veda's text and the living recitation are both real. They just begin in different places: one at the verse, the other at the doorway in front of it.
screen: `NOT IN THE RIG VEDA'S TEXT.` · `OM, THEN THREE UTTERANCES.` · `EARTH, THE SPACE BETWEEN, THE SKY.` · `A FRAME AROUND THE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause at the doorway. Sit, and let the breath settle. Before you begin the sit itself, stand at its threshold for three breaths. On the first out-breath, say silently: here. On the second: between. On the third: beyond. If you pray, you can use bhur, bhuvah, svah instead. Then step through, and simply rest, letting the breath come and go on its own. When the mind wanders off, come back to the doorway, take the three breaths again, and step through once more. The bell holds the time.
The Gayatri in context. In recitation, the verse is framed by Om and three utterances: earth, the space between, and the sky beyond. The Rig Veda's verse itself begins at tat savitur. Today's word.
Your line: the Gayatri in context. Today, before one thing you start, a call, a meal, a page, pause at its doorway for three breaths: here, between, beyond. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: In daily recitation, Hindus who chant the Gayatri may begin with Om and the three vyahritis, bhur bhuvah svah, before the verse itself; traditions vary on further additions.

myth: om bhur bhuvah svah is the first line of the Rig Veda verse
the verse begins tat savitur varenyam; the frame comes from recitation.
the Taittiriya Upanishad adds a fourth utterance, mahas
and it calls mahas the sun.
chanting the frame before the verse is a mistake
it's how the verse is recited in practice; the text and the recitation simply begin in different places.

fork.setup: you're about to recite the verse, framed. what comes right after Om?
fork.reveal: bhur bhuvah svah: earth, the space between, the sky. only then the verse to Savitr.

original.note: Sanskrit: an utterance; the name for bhur, bhuvah, svah, the words said before the Gayatri.

trapdoor: what you thought: om bhur bhuvah svah is part of the Gayatri verse.
what it means: it's a frame said before the verse in recitation; the Rig Veda's text begins at tat savitur.
what a scholar hears: the Taittiriya Upanishad names bhur, bhuvah, suvar as the three vyahritis, adds mahas as a fourth, and maps them onto earth, middle space, the world beyond, and the sun.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.5 (bhur, bhuvah, suvar, and mahas; this world, the middle space, the world beyond, the sun)

notes: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.5 paraphrase (three vyahritis plus mahas; bhur = this world, bhuvah = mid-space, suvar = yonder world, mahas = the sun) given from memory; confirm. The text also maps them to fire, wind, sun and moon, and to the Vedas; omitted here.

'Usually framed' and 'the shape most people hear' are general claims about practice; a Keeper may prefer 'often'. Some traditions add the further vyahritis or the 'apo jyoti' closing; left as 'some recitations go on to add more'.
Day 108 and other earlier days quote the Gayatri with the vyahritis as one line; this day explains the frame without contradicting them.
